BST260 Final Project Proposal

Betty Hou

Source: vignettes/proposal.qmd

Dear BST260 Teaching Team, Fall 2026,

I propose two analyses for my pkgdown site. The first links RAND’s firearm legislation records to CDC firearm mortality rates. The second examines the size of reported recreational-water outbreaks in CDC surveillance data.

State firearm background-check legislation and firearm mortality

Research question. Among U.S. states from 2014 through 2024, were age-adjusted firearm mortality rates different in years following a recorded restrictive background-check law change compared with years following no such change?

Data and population. The unit of analysis will be one state in one calendar year, covering the 50 states from 2014 through 2024. I will use the course package’s gunleg records from the RAND State Firearm Law Database and its cdcfiremort table from CDC’s National Center for Health Statistics. I will join the sources by state and year after standardizing state names and checking that the mortality table has one record per state-year.

Exposure and outcome. I will code exposure as 1 if RAND recorded at least one background-check law change classified as restrictive with an effective year immediately before the mortality year, and 0 if the available records show no qualifying change in that year. Multiple changes in one year will count as one exposure. I will check law IDs, effective years, and coding notes. If missing dates or classifications make a state-year’s exposure ambiguous, I will code it as missing and report how many observations I excluded. The outcome is the continuous CDC age-adjusted firearm death rate per 100,000 residents. I will report and exclude missing rates.

Analysis and adjustment. I will first plot the timing of qualifying changes and summarize mortality rates by exposure group. I will then estimate the adjusted difference in rates with a linear regression including state and year fixed effects, with uncertainty clustered by state. I chose state and year before fitting the model because long-standing differences between states and national trends may influence both legislative activity and firearm mortality. State-specific changes in other firearm laws, economic conditions, or earlier mortality trends could still confound the association. The exposure measures recent legislative activity, so the estimate describes an association with that activity.

Recreational-water treatment and reported outbreak size

Research question. Among recreational-water outbreaks reported to the CDC, did outbreaks linked exclusively to treated water have different numbers of reported illnesses than outbreaks linked exclusively to untreated water?

Data and population. The unit of analysis will be one reported U.S. outbreak in the course package’s waterborne extract from the CDC National Outbreak Reporting System. I will convert the nested list into one row per outbreak, check for duplicate record IDs, and retain records whose primary transmission mode is water. I will document the years and reporting locations represented in the extract.

Exposure and outcome. I will code water_exposure as treated or untreated using the corresponding single-category recreational-water labels. I will exclude records with missing or undetermined exposure, multiple water categories, or a different type of water exposure, and report the exclusions. The outcome is the number of reported illnesses per outbreak, a discrete quantitative count. I will preserve recorded zeroes and report and exclude missing or invalid illness counts.

Analysis and adjustment. I will use a reusable R function to summarize the number of outbreaks, median illness count, and interquartile range by exposure group and season. I will plot the distributions and use a count regression to estimate the adjusted ratio of expected illness counts. Before fitting the model, I chose season, calendar period, and U.S. Census region as adjustment variables because recreational-water use and outbreak detection can differ across seasons, years, and locations. I will derive season from the reported month and report missing adjustment values. The findings will apply to reported outbreaks. The dataset does not provide the number of people exposed to each water type, so I will estimate outbreak size rather than individual illness risk.
